newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Iran row highlights EU foreign policy dilemma.
newsitem.headline: Iran row highlights EU foreign policy dilemma.

text.p: The European Union's conflicting responses to two major foreign issues in one week highlight the 15-member bloc's problems in trying to forge a consistent common foreign policy in a world where commerce is often king.

In taking a common tough stance and cutting off "critical dialogue" with Tehran, the EU has moved into line with the United States and sacrificed the commercial potential of maintaining relations with oil-rich Iran.
It also exorcised to some extent last weekend's internal rift over whether to condemn China's human rights record.

Europe's swift action against Iran followed a German court finding on Thursday that Iran's political leadership ordered the killings of a group of Iranian Kurdish leaders in a Berlin restaurant in 1992.
Germany, Iran's largest trading partner and most important Western friend, ordered four Iranian diplomats to leave the country and recalled its ambassador in Tehran.
The move was quickly endorsed by the EU which invited its members to withdraw top diplomats and said it saw no room for the "critical dialogue" it has had with Iran for five years.

Britain, which has argued for a tough policy towards Iran because of its record on terrorism, human rights and a Fatwa against writer Salman Rushdie, said on Friday it would withdraw its charge-d'affaires from Tehran shortly.
Diplomatic sources in Brussels said other EU members were expected to follow suit during Friday.
The United States, which has long argued that Europe is motivated by commercial greed for deals in Iran, applauded the suspension of critical dialogue which it says is fruitless.

Iran has been a major bone of contention between Washington and its European allies. The EU has refused to join U.S. trade sanctions on Iran and has attacked U.S. legislation cracking down on firms that invest in the oil or gas industry there.

"We hope the European Union will join the United States in a realistic policy that is aimed at containing Iran and containing its ability to further destabilise the Middle East and to murder its own citizens abroad," the U.S. said on Thursday.
Tehran denies that it supports terrorism.
Last weekend, attempts to move towards a common EU foreign policy were left in tatters when France refused to back an EU resolution condemning China's record on human rights.

Paris, swayed by Beijing's moves towards accepting U.N. human rights standards and by the prospect of lucrative export deals, distanced itself from its EU colleagues, arguing that dialogue with China was better than confrontation.

After Germany, Spain and Italy backed France, it was left to Denmark, supported by the United States and other EU members, to table a censure against China at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva.

With President Jacques Chirac due to visit China next month, France also said it hoped the EU could lift an arms sales ban imposed after Beijing crushed student-led pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square in 1989.
China praised Paris for not joining the EU rights motion and hinted that this would boost French business with China.
